sections.title: 1. Escaping Flatland: Electron Domains & VSEPR Repulsion
sections.summary: Discover why flat 2D Lewis structures act like subway maps—showing which atoms connect, while hiding real 3D molecular shape. Using simple electrostatic repulsion between negatively charged electron clouds, learn how Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory predicts the farthest-apart 3D arrangement by counting every single bond, multiple bond, or lone pair around a central atom as one compact electron domain.
introduced_terms: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory

chunks.title: Why Lewis Drawings Are Like Subway Maps
chunks.content_markdown:
If you have ever navigated a big city using a subway map, you know a helpful secret: the map tells you which stations connect, not the true twists and distances of the tunnels underground. A **Lewis structure**—a flat dot-and-line drawing showing how atoms arrange their **valence electrons** (their outermost, bonding-ready electrons)—works the exact same way.

In a Lewis drawing, each line represents a **covalent bond** (a pair of valence electrons shared between two atoms), and each pair of unshared dots represents a **lone pair** resting on a single atom. Chemists routinely sketch methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) as a flat plus sign and water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) as a straight horizontal line simply because paper and screens are flat. Yet real molecules live in three-dimensional space, and their true 3D shapes decide everything from why water beads on a leaf to how scents fit inside your nose.

questions.prompt: Why is a flat Lewis structure best compared to a city subway map?
choices: It shows exact three-dimensional bond angles but hides which atoms are linked.
It accurately displays atom-to-atom connectivity while distorting real 3D geometry.
It tracks only unshared lone pairs while leaving out shared covalent bonds.
It works only for gaseous molecules rather than liquids or crystalline solids.
questions.explanation: Like a subway map, a Lewis structure reliably reveals which atoms are connected and where electrons sit, even though flattening it onto paper distorts true 3D angles.

questions.prompt: In a Lewis drawing, what is the difference between a covalent bond and a lone pair?
choices: A covalent bond sits on one atom alone, whereas a lone pair connects two nuclei.
A covalent bond contains inner core electrons, whereas a lone pair holds protons.
A covalent bond is shared between two atoms, whereas a lone pair belongs to one atom.
A covalent bond determines 3D shape, whereas a lone pair has no spatial effect.
questions.explanation: A covalent bond consists of valence electrons shared between two atoms, whereas a lone pair is a pair of valence electrons localized on a single atom.

chunks.title: Balloon Physics and VSEPR Repulsion
chunks.content_markdown:
How do molecules choose their real three-dimensional shapes? You do not need advanced math to figure it out—you just need one familiar rule of electricity. Because every electron carries a negative electric charge, negatively charged electron clouds push away from one another through **Coulomb repulsion** (the electrostatic force that drives like charges apart).

That simple push is the entire engine behind **Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory**, usually pronounced 'vesper.' VSEPR states that the outer electron clouds surrounding a central atom automatically spread out into whichever 3D arrangement places them as far apart as possible. Imagine tying several inflated party balloons together at their necks. Without anyone measuring an angle, the balloons elbow one another aside until every balloon claims maximum personal space. Electron clouds around an atom behave just like those knotted balloons, settling naturally into the lowest-repulsion 3D geometry.

questions.prompt: What physical force drives a molecule into its preferred VSEPR three-dimensional shape?
choices: Gravitational pull drawing heavier outer atoms downward toward the bottom.
Magnetic alignment locking all outer bonds parallel to Earth's magnetic poles.
Electrostatic attraction pulling neighboring valence electron clouds closer together.
Coulomb repulsion pushing negatively charged outer electron clouds far apart.
questions.explanation: Because valence electron clouds are all negatively charged, Coulomb repulsion forces them into the 3D arrangement that maximizes their separation.

questions.prompt: In the knotted-balloon analogy for VSEPR theory, what do the inflated balloons represent?
choices: Regions of negatively charged outer electron density crowding around a central atom.
Positively charged atomic nuclei floating freely without any chemical bonds.
Rigid wooden sticks forcing atoms to stay locked inside a flat two-dimensional grid.
Deep inner-shell electrons buried too close to the nucleus to interact.
questions.explanation: Each balloon models a valence electron cloud tethered to the central atom; just as balloons push apart for room, electron clouds repel into symmetric 3D layouts.

chunks.title: Counting Electron Domains and Steric Number
chunks.content_markdown:
To put VSEPR to work, we first need a clean way to count how many 'balloons' are tied to a central atom. Chemists call each distinct pocket of outer electron density around a central atom an **electron domain** (sometimes called a steric cloud, where 'steric' simply refers to 3D space and physical crowding). Both a covalent bond pointing toward a neighbor and a lone pair sitting on the central atom take up real physical space, so each counts as one electron domain.

Adding up all the electron domains around a central atom gives its **steric number**. Let us try three everyday molecules. In methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$), carbon forms four single bonds to hydrogen and has zero lone pairs, giving a steric number of $$4$$. In ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$), nitrogen forms three single bonds and keeps one lone pair—also a steric number of $$4$$. In water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$), oxygen forms two single bonds and holds two lone pairs—once again, a steric number of $$4$$!

questions.prompt: What does the steric number of a central atom count?
choices: The total number of protons inside the central atom's nucleus.
The total number of electron domains surrounding that central atom.
The total number of outer atoms minus any unshared lone pairs.
The total molecular weight of every atom attached to the center.
questions.explanation: The steric number is simply the count of all electron domains—both bonding regions and lone pairs—arranged around a given central atom.

questions.prompt: Why do methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$), ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$), and water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) all share a steric number of $$4$$?
choices: Each central atom is surrounded by four identical single bonds to hydrogen.
Each molecule contains exactly four total atoms in its chemical formula.
Each central atom holds four total electron domains when bonds and lone pairs are summed.
Each central atom carries four unshared lone pairs in its outer valence shell.
questions.explanation: Counting bonds plus lone pairs gives $$4+0=4$$ for $$\text{CH}_4$$, $$3+1=4$$ for $$\text{NH}_3$$, and $$2+2=4$$ for $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$.

chunks.title: The Multiple-Bond Surprise: One Direction, One Domain
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is the most common stumbling block when people first learn to count electron domains: what do you do with a **double bond** (two shared electron pairs) or a **triple bond** (three shared electron pairs) linking the same two atoms? It is tempting to count a double bond as two separate domains, yet VSEPR treats every multiple bond as just **one** electron domain.

Why? Think physically about where those electrons live. All the shared electrons in a double or triple bond are locked in the exact same corridor between the same two nuclei—they cannot swing apart to opposite sides of the central atom like separate balloons! In carbon dioxide ($$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$$), the central carbon has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so its steric number is $$2$$, not $$4$$. Similarly, in formaldehyde ($$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$), carbon has two single bonds to hydrogen and one double bond to oxygen, giving a steric number of $$3$$.

questions.prompt: Why does a double bond between two atoms count as only one electron domain in VSEPR?
choices: The second shared pair carries a neutral charge and creates no repulsion.
Both shared pairs stay trapped in the same single direction between those two nuclei.
Double bonds are too short to interact with neighboring bonds or lone pairs.
One of the two shared pairs moves into the inner core shell after bonding.
questions.explanation: Because all electrons in a double or triple bond occupy the same region between the same two atoms, they act as one unified steric cloud pointing in one direction.

questions.prompt: In hydrogen cyanide ($$\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$$), carbon has one single bond, one triple bond, and no lone pairs. What is carbon's steric number?
choices: $$2$$, because the single bond and triple bond form two electron domains.
$$3$$, because only the three shared pairs in the triple bond count.
$$4$$, because carbon shares four total pairs of valence electrons.
$$1$$, because both bonds connect along the same central carbon atom.
questions.explanation: One single bond counts as 1 electron domain and one triple bond counts as 1 electron domain, giving carbon a steric number of $$2$$.

chunks.title: Your VSEPR Launchpad
chunks.content_markdown:
You now hold the master key that unlocks three-dimensional chemistry. Rather than memorizing a giant wall of molecular formulas, VSEPR lets you start from any valid Lewis structure, pick a central atom, and ask one physical question: how many separate electron clouds are jostling for space around this center?

Remember our three simple counting rules. Every single bond counts as one electron domain. Every lone pair on the central atom counts as one electron domain. And every double or triple bond—no matter how many electron pairs it packs between two nuclei—still points in one direction and counts as just one electron domain. Once you know that steric number, Coulomb repulsion handles the rest automatically. In the next section, we will watch what happens when $$2$$, $$3$$, or $$4$$ electron domains push as far apart as three-dimensional space allows, sculpting the core frameworks behind nearly all organic and biological molecules.

questions.prompt: A central atom in a Lewis structure has one double bond, one single bond, and one lone pair. What is its steric number?
choices: $$2$$, because lone pairs do not contribute to the steric number.
$$4$$, because the double bond counts as two separate steric clouds.
$$5$$, because every individual valence electron counts as a domain.
$$3$$, because the double bond, single bond, and lone pair each form one domain.
questions.explanation: Counting each region of electron density gives 1 (double bond) + 1 (single bond) + 1 (lone pair) = steric number $$3$$.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes the first steps of predicting a molecule's 3D geometry with VSEPR?
choices: Weigh the outer atoms first, then arrange the heaviest ones on the bottom.
Start from a valid Lewis structure, then count all electron domains around the central atom.
Ignore any lone pairs on the central atom, then double the count of multiple bonds.
Draw the molecule flat on grid paper, then measure every corner at $$90^\circ$$.
questions.explanation: VSEPR begins with a valid Lewis structure so you can accurately tally all bonding domains and lone pairs around the central atom.

sections.title: 2. The Core 3D Frameworks: Linear, Trigonal Planar & Tetrahedral
sections.summary: Build the three workhorse electron-domain architectures that underlie nearly all organic and biological molecules through pure spatial intuition—no trigonometry required. Follow how 2 domains push to opposite sides in a linear $$180^\circ$$ line ($$\text{CO}_2$$), 3 domains fan into a flat trigonal planar $$120^\circ$$ triangle ($$\text{BF}_3$$, $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$), and 4 domains break out of flat $$90^\circ$$ paper squares into a three-dimensional tetrahedral $$109.5^\circ$$ tripod ($$\text{CH}_4$$).

chunks.title: The 90-Degree Illusion on Flat Paper
chunks.content_markdown:
Look at a standard Lewis drawing of methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$): one carbon sitting in the center with four hydrogen atoms sticking straight up, down, left, and right like the spokes of a compass. Looking at that flat cross, anyone would guess that the angle between neighboring carbon-hydrogen bonds is $$90^\circ$$. Yet when scientists measure real methane molecules in the lab, every single angle between two hydrogens is a roomy $$109.5^\circ$$!

Where did those extra $$19.5^\circ$$ of breathing room come from? Flat paper trapped the four electron domains inside a two-dimensional circle of $$360^\circ$$, where four equal slices can never exceed $$90^\circ$$. Real molecules are not pinned to a sheet of paper. When four negatively charged clouds escape upward and downward into full three-dimensional space, they instantly relieve crowding. Before jumping to four domains, let us watch what happens as we tie $$2$$, $$3$$, and then $$4$$ balloons together one by one.

questions.prompt: Why are the actual bond angles in methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) much wider than the $$90^\circ$$ angles shown in a flat Lewis drawing?
choices: Hydrogen atoms attract one another magnetically until they swing wider.
Escaping from a flat plane into 3D space lets the four electron domains spread farther apart.
Carbon shrinks its nucleus during bonding to open up room on a flat circle.
Two of the four carbon-hydrogen bonds vanish briefly to relieve steric crowding.
questions.explanation: On a flat 2D plane, four equal regions are capped at $$90^\circ$$, but lifting out into 3D space allows all four domains to separate to $$109.5^\circ$$.

questions.prompt: What geometric limit traps four equally spaced lines drawn on a flat sheet of paper?
choices: A flat circle holds $$360^\circ$$ total, capping four equal slices at $$90^\circ$$ each.
A flat circle holds $$180^\circ$$ total, capping four equal slices at $$45^\circ$$ each.
A flat circle forces opposite lines to bend inward to $$109.5^\circ$$ each.
A flat circle forbids placing more than three lines around a single point.
questions.explanation: Dividing a flat $$360^\circ$$ circle into four equal parts can yield at most $$90^\circ$$ per gap, which is why flat drawings underestimate 3D separation.

chunks.title: Two and Three Domains: Straight Lines and Flat Triangles
chunks.content_markdown:
Start with the simplest case: a steric number of $$2$$. Imagine tying just two inflated balloons together at their necks. To stay as far apart as possible, they point in exact opposite directions along a straight line. Chemists call this **linear geometry (180 degrees)**. No matter how you twist it in 3D space, you can never get two domains farther apart than $$180^\circ$$.

Now tie a third balloon into the knot for a steric number of $$3$$. All three balloons push apart equally until they fan out like the three blades of a ceiling fan or the corners of an equilateral triangle. Because every balloon lies in the same flat plane, chemists call this **trigonal planar geometry (120 degrees)**. Why does a 3-domain molecule stay flat instead of popping upward into a tent? Bending all three blades slightly upward would actually pull them closer to one another, increasing Coulomb repulsion instead of reducing it.

questions.prompt: What electron-domain geometry and ideal angle occur when a central atom has a steric number of $$2$$?
choices: Trigonal planar geometry with a $$120^\circ$$ separation.
Bent geometry with a $$90^\circ$$ separation.
Linear geometry with a $$180^\circ$$ separation.
Tetrahedral geometry with a $$109.5^\circ$$ separation.
questions.explanation: Two electron domains maximize their separation by pointing directly opposite one another in a linear $$180^\circ$$ arrangement.

questions.prompt: Why do three electron domains stay in a flat $$120^\circ$$ triangle instead of tilting upward into a 3D cone?
choices: Electron clouds around three-domain atoms are too heavy to lift out of a plane.
Three-domain molecules cannot rotate freely once they form covalent bonds.
Coulomb repulsion disappears completely whenever angles drop below $$120^\circ$$.
Tilting the three domains upward pulls them closer together and raises repulsion.
questions.explanation: A flat equilateral triangle maximizes the angle between three domains at $$120^\circ$$; lifting them out of the plane shrinks the angles between them.

chunks.title: Four Domains Break Into 3D: The Tetrahedron
chunks.content_markdown:
When we tie a fourth balloon into our knot (steric number $$4$$), flat geometry finally breaks down. If four domains tried to stay flat in a $$90^\circ$$ square, they would sit uncomfortably close. Instead, two domains swing upward and forward while the other two swing downward and back, forming **tetrahedral geometry (109.5 degrees)**—a perfectly balanced 3D tripod with one leg pointing straight up and three legs splayed downward like a camera stand.

Let us walk through classic molecules for all three frameworks. Carbon dioxide ($$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$$) has $$2$$ domains around carbon, making it **linear** ($$180^\circ$$). Boron trifluoride ($$\text{BF}_3$$) has $$3$$ single-bond domains around boron, making it **trigonal planar** ($$120^\circ$$). And methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) has $$4$$ single-bond domains around carbon, making it **tetrahedral**—with every single $$\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{H}$$ pair separated by an identical $$109.5^\circ$$.

questions.prompt: In a tetrahedral molecule like methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$), how do the four $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bond directions compare?
choices: Two bonds lie at $$180^\circ$$ while the other two sit squeezed at $$90^\circ$$.
All four bonds are geometrically equivalent, with every pair separated by $$109.5^\circ$$.
Three bonds form a flat $$120^\circ$$ base while one top bond sits at $$90^\circ$$.
All four bonds stay flat in one square plane with $$109.5^\circ$$ corners.
questions.explanation: A regular tetrahedron is completely symmetric: all four corners are equivalent, and every pair of bonds forms an identical $$109.5^\circ$$ angle.

questions.prompt: Match each molecule—$$\text{CO}_2$$, $$\text{BF}_3$$, and $$\text{CH}_4$$—to its electron-domain geometry in order.
choices: Trigonal planar, linear, and tetrahedral.
Tetrahedral, trigonal planar, and linear.
Linear, tetrahedral, and trigonal planar.
Linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral.
questions.explanation: Counting domains gives $$2$$ (linear) for $$\text{CO}_2$$, $$3$$ (trigonal planar) for $$\text{BF}_3$$, and $$4$$ (tetrahedral) for $$\text{CH}_4$$.

chunks.title: Spot the Geometry Trap: Double Bonds Inside Flat Triangles
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a subtle trap that catches many newcomers off guard. Consider formaldehyde ($$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$), a simple molecule where a central carbon atom is bonded to two hydrogens by single bonds and to one oxygen by a double bond, with zero lone pairs. Because carbon forms four total bonding pairs—just like in methane—people often assume formaldehyde must be tetrahedral.

Wait a second! Remember our golden rule from Section 1: a double bond occupies a single corridor between carbon and oxygen, so it counts as just **one** electron domain. Tallying the domains around formaldehyde's carbon gives one domain for the first $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bond, one for the second $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bond, and one for the $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bond—a steric number of $$3$$. As a result, formaldehyde is completely flat and **trigonal planar**, with angles right near $$120^\circ$$ rather than a 3D tetrahedron.

questions.prompt: Why is formaldehyde ($$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$) flat and trigonal planar instead of tetrahedral like methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$)?
choices: Its oxygen atom pulls the two hydrogens flat through gravitational attraction.
Its carbon atom has three electron domains because the double bond counts as one.
Its carbon atom violates VSEPR by placing four domains in a flat circle.
Its two hydrogen atoms fuse together into one shared bonding electron domain.
questions.explanation: Two single bonds plus one double bond give carbon a steric number of $$3$$, producing a flat trigonal planar framework near $$120^\circ$$.

questions.prompt: Carbon has four shared electron pairs in both $$\text{CO}_2$$ ($$\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$$) and $$\text{CH}_4$$. Why are their shapes completely different?
choices: Oxygen atoms cannot form bond angles smaller than $$180^\circ$$ in any compound.
Hydrogen atoms are too lightweight to form linear molecules with central carbon.
Coulomb repulsion acts only on single bonds and ignores every double bond.
Those four pairs form $$2$$ domains in $$\text{CO}_2$$ versus $$4$$ domains in $$\text{CH}_4$$.
questions.explanation: Shape depends on the number of separate electron domains ($$2$$ linear domains in $$\text{CO}_2$$ vs. $$4$$ tetrahedral domains in $$\text{CH}_4$$), not the total number of shared electron pairs.

chunks.title: The Three Pillars of Organic Architecture
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause and appreciate how much chemical territory you already command with just three intuitive balloon arrangements. Almost every molecule in your body—sugars, fats, DNA, proteins, and medicines—is built from carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen centers whose steric numbers are $$2$$, $$3$$, or $$4$$. Two domains snap straight into a $$180^\circ$$ linear rod. Three domains fan flat into a $$120^\circ$$ trigonal planar triangle. Four domains pop into a $$109.5^\circ$$ tetrahedral tripod.

So far, every example we examined—$$\text{CO}_2$$, $$\text{BF}_3$$, $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$, and $$\text{CH}_4$$—had zero lone pairs on its central atom, meaning every balloon ended in a visible atom. But what happens when a central atom like nitrogen in ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) or oxygen in water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) replaces one or two of those bonded atoms with unshared lone pairs? In Section 3, we will watch those invisible balloons sculpt bent and pyramidal shapes.

questions.prompt: Which three steric numbers form the core geometric frameworks of nearly all organic and biological molecules?
choices: Steric numbers $$1$$, $$2$$, and $$3$$ only.
Steric numbers $$2$$, $$3$$, and $$4$$.
Steric numbers $$4$$, $$5$$, and $$6$$.
Steric numbers $$3$$, $$5$$, and $$7$$.
questions.explanation: Carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen in organic and biological molecules overwhelmingly adopt steric numbers $$2$$ (linear), $$3$$ (trigonal planar), and $$4$$ (tetrahedral).

questions.prompt: What special feature did $$\text{CO}_2$$, $$\text{BF}_3$$, $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$, and $$\text{CH}_4$$ all share in this section?
choices: Every one of them contained at least one double bond to oxygen.
Every one of them stayed completely flat inside a two-dimensional plane.
Every one of them had zero lone pairs on its central atom.
Every one of them held an identical steric number of $$4$$.
questions.explanation: None of these central atoms had lone pairs, so every electron domain ended in a visible outer atom; Section 3 explores what changes when lone pairs are present.

sections.title: 3. Invisible Sculptors: Electron-Domain vs. Molecular Geometry
sections.summary: Separate the full, invisible electron-domain framework from the visible molecular geometry traced out only by atomic nuclei. Watch nonbonding lone pairs act like invisible balloons that occupy real space and push bonded atoms aside—sculpting bent $$\text{SO}_2$$ from a 3-domain frame, trigonal pyramidal $$\text{NH}_3$$ from a 4-domain frame, and bent $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ instead of a straight line.

chunks.title: The Tale of Two Three-Atom Molecules
chunks.content_markdown:
Look at two of the most famous three-atom molecules on Earth: carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$) and water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$). On paper, their formulas look like twins—one central atom flanked by two identical outer atoms. You might naturally assume both molecules should stretch out into tidy straight lines. Yet nature disagrees dramatically: $$\text{CO}_2$$ is ruler-straight at $$180^\circ$$, whereas $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ is sharply kinked into a boomerang-like V shape!

That bend is no tiny quirk—it is the reason liquid water exists at room temperature, why ice floats on lakes, and why life works at all. What invisible force bends water's two hydrogen atoms downward while letting carbon dioxide's two oxygens stretch straight out? The culprit is hiding right on oxygen's head in the Lewis structure: two unshared **lone pairs** that claim real 3D space even though no outer atom sits at their tips.

questions.prompt: Although $$\text{CO}_2$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ both have one central atom and two outer atoms, why do they have different 3D shapes?
choices: Oxygen's two lone pairs occupy 3D space and push water's hydrogens into a bend.
Hydrogen atoms are too light to balance on opposite sides of an oxygen nucleus.
Carbon dioxide contains no valence electrons anywhere on its outer oxygen atoms.
Water forms triple bonds that twist its two hydrogen atoms toward the same side.
questions.explanation: Carbon in $$\text{CO}_2$$ has zero lone pairs (steric number $$2$$, linear), whereas oxygen in $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ has two lone pairs (steric number $$4$$) that push the hydrogens into a bent shape.

questions.prompt: Why does drawing water ($$\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H}$$) straight across a page mislead a reader about its real geometry?
choices: It implies oxygen forms double bonds rather than single bonds to hydrogen.
It hides the spatial crowding created by oxygen's two unshared lone pairs.
It suggests that water contains three separate central atoms instead of one.
It exaggerates the length of each oxygen-hydrogen bond by ten times.
questions.explanation: A straight-line drawing ignores the two lone-pair domains on oxygen, which force the molecule into an angular V shape in three dimensions.

chunks.title: Invisible Balloons: Electron-Domain vs. Molecular Geometry
chunks.content_markdown:
To talk clearly about lone pairs without ever getting confused, chemists make a crisp distinction between **electron-domain geometry vs. molecular geometry**. Return to our knotted-balloon picture. Imagine tying four balloons together into a symmetric tetrahedron. That full four-balloon layout—counting both bonding pairs and lone pairs—is the **electron-domain geometry**.

Now imagine waving a magic wand that turns one of those four balloons completely transparent! The invisible balloon is still inflated, still solid, and still shoving the other three balloons firmly into place, so the remaining three balloons cannot flatten out. Yet when an experimental probe takes a snapshot of the atoms, it only sees the atomic nuclei at the ends of the visible bonds. That visible skeleton of atoms alone is the **molecular geometry**. Lone pairs are invisible sculptors: you do not name them in the final shape, but their footprints shape every angle you see.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry?
choices: Electron-domain geometry ignores lone pairs, while molecular geometry includes them.
Electron-domain geometry applies to gases, while molecular geometry applies to solids.
Electron-domain geometry maps all domains, while molecular geometry describes only the atoms.
Electron-domain geometry uses 2D drawings, while molecular geometry uses 3D models.
questions.explanation: Electron-domain geometry tracks every bonding and lone-pair domain around the center, whereas molecular geometry names the visible arrangement of the atomic nuclei alone.

questions.prompt: In the invisible-balloon analogy, why do the remaining visible bonds refuse to flatten out when a lone pair replaces a bonded atom?
choices: The visible bonds grow heavier and droop downward under gravity.
The central nucleus rotates faster and locks the bonds into place.
The remaining outer atoms bond directly to one another to form a ring.
The invisible lone-pair cloud still occupies space and repels neighboring bonds.
questions.explanation: Even though a lone pair has no atom at its tip, its negatively charged electron cloud still repels neighboring bonds just like an invisible inflated balloon.

chunks.title: Sculpting Ammonia and Water from a Tetrahedron
chunks.content_markdown:
Let us watch those invisible sculptors carve two iconic molecules out of the exact same 4-domain tetrahedral framework. Start with ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$). Nitrogen has three single bonds to hydrogen and one lone pair, giving a steric number of $$4$$ and a **tetrahedral** electron-domain geometry. Now hide the single lone pair sitting on top of the nitrogen. Look at the four visible atoms left behind: nitrogen perched slightly above a triangular base of three hydrogens, like a tiny three-legged camera tripod. Chemists call this **trigonal pyramidal geometry**.

Next, move one step further to water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$). Oxygen has two single bonds to hydrogen and two lone pairs—still steric number $$4$$, still a **tetrahedral** electron-domain geometry! Turn both lone-pair balloons invisible, and only two legs of the tetrahedron remain visible. Those two bonds meet at a crisp corner, giving water its **bent (angular) molecular geometry**.

questions.prompt: What are the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry of ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$)?
choices: Trigonal planar electron-domain geometry and trigonal planar molecular geometry.
Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.
Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and bent molecular geometry.
Trigonal pyramidal electron-domain geometry and linear molecular geometry.
questions.explanation: With 3 bonds and 1 lone pair (4 total domains), $$\text{NH}_3$$ has a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, leaving a trigonal pyramidal arrangement of its atoms.

questions.prompt: Why does ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) form a raised pyramid rather than a flat triangle like $$\text{BF}_3$$?
choices: Nitrogen's lone pair occupies the fourth tetrahedral spot and pushes the three hydrogens downward.
Hydrogen atoms are larger than fluorine atoms and collide if placed in one flat plane.
Ammonia contains three double bonds that tilt the molecule out of a flat plane.
Nitrogen has a steric number of $$3$$, which always bends downward into a cone.
questions.explanation: Unlike boron in $$\text{BF}_3$$ (steric number $$3$$, zero lone pairs), nitrogen in $$\text{NH}_3$$ has a lone pair (steric number $$4$$) pushing the three bonds below the plane.

chunks.title: Two Roads to 'Bent': Comparing Sulfur Dioxide and Water
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a neat twist that trips up rote memorizers but feels effortless once you picture balloons: not every **bent** molecule comes from a tetrahedron! Consider sulfur dioxide ($$\text{SO}_2$$), the sharp-smelling gas released by volcanoes. In its Lewis structure, the central sulfur atom is bonded to two oxygens (with bonding shared across both sides) and carries **one** lone pair.

Count sulfur's electron domains: two oxygen-bonding directions plus one lone pair equals a steric number of $$3$$! That gives $$\text{SO}_2$$ a flat **trigonal planar** electron-domain geometry with ideal $$120^\circ$$ corners. When we turn that single lone-pair balloon invisible, the two remaining sulfur-oxygen bonds form a **bent (angular) molecular geometry**—just like water, yet built from a 3-domain triangle rather than a 4-domain tetrahedron! Because it starts from a roomier $$120^\circ$$ frame instead of a $$109.5^\circ$$ frame, $$\text{SO}_2$$ has a noticeably wider bend than $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$.

questions.prompt: What are the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry of sulfur dioxide ($$\text{SO}_2$$)?
choices: Linear electron-domain geometry and linear molecular geometry.
Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.
Trigonal planar electron-domain geometry and bent molecular geometry.
Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry and bent molecular geometry.
questions.explanation: Sulfur in $$\text{SO}_2$$ has 2 bonding domains and 1 lone pair (steric number $$3$$), giving a trigonal planar domain frame and a bent molecular shape.

questions.prompt: Why is the bend angle in $$\text{SO}_2$$ wider than the bend angle in $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$?
choices: $$\text{SO}_2$$ has zero lone pairs on sulfur, whereas $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ has one.
Sulfur atoms always force neighboring covalent bonds closer to $$180^\circ$$.
$$\text{SO}_2$$ sits on a 4-domain frame, while $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ uses a 3-domain frame.
$$\text{SO}_2$$ starts from a $$120^\circ$$ triangle, whereas $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ starts from a $$109.5^\circ$$ tetrahedron.
questions.explanation: Because $$\text{SO}_2$$ has steric number $$3$$ (starting from $$120^\circ$$) and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ has steric number $$4$$ (starting from $$109.5^\circ$$), $$\text{SO}_2$$ opens wider.

chunks.title: Seeing the Unseen in Every Molecule
chunks.content_markdown:
With one simple mental shift—separating the invisible balloon frame from the visible atomic skeleton—you have unlocked every shape across steric numbers $$2$$, $$3$$, and $$4$$ without memorizing a single lookup table. Whenever a central atom has zero lone pairs, its electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry match identically: linear, trigonal planar, or tetrahedral. Whenever lone pairs appear, simply keep the exact same electron-domain frame, make the lone-pair balloons transparent, and name the visible shape left behind: bent from $$3$$ domains ($$\text{SO}_2$$), trigonal pyramidal from $$4$$ domains with one lone pair ($$\text{NH}_3$$), or bent from $$4$$ domains with two lone pairs ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$).

Now that you can picture these 3D pyramids and tetrahedra clearly in your head, one practical problem remains: how do chemists draw them on flat paper without losing their depth? Section 4 introduces the sleek wedge-and-dash shorthand that solves that puzzle effortlessly.

questions.prompt: When do a central atom's electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry have the exact same name?
choices: Whenever the central atom carries at least one lone pair.
Whenever the molecule contains only two atoms in total.
Whenever the central atom has zero lone pairs.
Whenever the central atom forms at least one double bond.
questions.explanation: If there are zero lone pairs on the central atom, every electron domain terminates in a visible atom, so the electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry match.

questions.prompt: An unfamiliar molecule has a central atom with $$3$$ bonding domains and $$1$$ lone pair. Without consulting a chart, what is its molecular geometry?
choices: Trigonal planar, because there are three outer atoms bonded to the center.
Bent, because any lone pair reduces a molecule to a two-legged shape.
Tetrahedral, because four electron domains always produce a tetrahedral molecular shape.
Trigonal pyramidal, because hiding one tetrahedral corner leaves a three-legged pyramid.
questions.explanation: Four total domains establish a tetrahedral frame; turning the single lone-pair domain invisible leaves a three-legged trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry.

sections.title: 4. Drawing Depth on Paper: Reading Wedge-and-Dash 3D Perspective
sections.summary: Learn to read and sketch organic chemistry's effortless 3D shorthand on a flat page without needing artistic talent. Using plain lines for bonds lying in the plane of the page, solid wedges for bonds jutting toward you, and hashed dashes for bonds receding behind the page, practice mentally turning everyday tetrahedral molecules like $$\text{CH}_4$$, $$\text{NH}_3$$, and $$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$$ to recognize identical 3D shapes from different viewpoints.

chunks.title: Putting 3D Molecules Back Onto Flat Paper
chunks.content_markdown:
Linear molecules like $$\text{CO}_2$$ and flat trigonal planar molecules like $$\text{BF}_3$$ are easy to draw on a whiteboard because every atom already lies in one flat plane. The moment you hit a tetrahedral molecule like methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) or a trigonal pyramidal molecule like ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$), flat lines suddenly fail you—some bonds need to poke right out of the page toward your face while others duck behind it.

Most chemists are scientists, not Renaissance portrait painters, so they needed a fast, unmistakable visual shorthand for depth. That shorthand is the **wedge-and-dash projection**, a universal drawing convention used in virtually every organic chemistry textbook, medicine label, and research paper on Earth. With just three simple stroke styles, a flat drawing instantly pops into three-dimensional perspective, letting any reader reconstruct the exact 3D arrangement in their mind's eye.

questions.prompt: Why do chemists need wedge-and-dash drawings for tetrahedral molecules like $$\text{CH}_4$$, but rarely for $$\text{CO}_2$$ or $$\text{BF}_3$$?
choices: Because $$\text{CH}_4$$ has bonds pointing in front of and behind any single flat plane.
Because $$\text{CO}_2$$ and $$\text{BF}_3$$ contain double bonds that cannot be drawn with lines.
Because hydrogen atoms are too small to appear clearly on flat paper.
Because linear and trigonal planar molecules change shape too quickly to draw.
questions.explanation: Linear and trigonal planar molecules already sit flat in one plane, whereas tetrahedral and pyramidal molecules extend outward in three dimensions.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a wedge-and-dash projection in chemistry?
choices: To measure the exact atomic mass of every element in a compound.
To replace chemical element symbols with abstract geometric icons.
To distinguish covalent bonds from unshared lone pairs by color.
To show the three-dimensional depth of bonds clearly on a flat page.
questions.explanation: A wedge-and-dash projection communicates 3D spatial orientation on a 2D surface using simple line, wedge, and dash conventions.

chunks.title: Three Simple Strokes: Lines, Wedges, and Dashes
chunks.content_markdown:
Reading a wedge-and-dash drawing takes less than thirty seconds to master because all three strokes copy how human eyes naturally read depth. First, a plain straight **in-plane bond line** indicates a bond lying completely flat inside the sheet of paper or screen—neither reaching toward you nor tilting away.

Next come the two depth strokes: the **solid wedge (forward) and hashed dash (receding)**. A bold, solid dark wedge starts narrow at the central atom and flares wider as it approaches the outer atom, just like a highway growing wider as it rushes toward you; it means that bond is jutting forward out of the page toward your eyes. A hashed (striped) wedge made of stacked parallel dashes fades into the distance like the receding rungs of a ladder; it means that bond is pointing backward behind the page, away from you.

questions.prompt: In a wedge-and-dash drawing, what does a solid dark wedge represent?
choices: A bond lying completely flat inside the plane of the page.
A double bond containing two shared pairs of valence electrons.
A bond projecting forward out of the page toward the viewer.
A weak bond that is currently breaking apart during a reaction.
questions.explanation: A solid wedge widens toward the viewer like an object coming closer, signaling a bond pointing forward out of the plane of the page.

questions.prompt: How do an in-plane bond line and a hashed dash differ in 3D orientation?
choices: The in-plane line points toward you, while the hashed dash lies flat on the page.
The in-plane line lies flat in the page, while the hashed dash recedes behind the page.
The in-plane line shows a lone pair, while the hashed dash shows a triple bond.
The in-plane line points upward, while the hashed dash points straight downward.
questions.explanation: Plain lines lie in the plane of the drawing surface, whereas hashed dashes indicate bonds angling backward behind the plane.

chunks.title: Sketching Methane and Ammonia in True 3D
chunks.content_markdown:
Let us build a clean 3D snapshot of tetrahedral methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) step by step. Start by drawing carbon in the middle and placing two of its $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bonds flat in the page as plain lines—say, one pointing straight up and one angling down to the left—forming a wide $$109.5^\circ$$ V shape. Those two plain lines define the flat plane of your paper.

Where do the other two hydrogens go? Because all four corners of a tetrahedron push as far apart as possible, both remaining bonds must sprout from the **wide outside** of that in-plane V, angling down to the right—one poking forward toward you as a solid wedge, and the other angling away behind the page as a hashed dash. Now erase the top upright hydrogen of methane and leave nitrogen's lone pair in its place: instantly you are looking at a crisp 3D tripod of trigonal pyramidal ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$)!

questions.prompt: In the standard wedge-and-dash drawing of tetrahedral methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$), how are the four bonds distributed?
choices: Two in-plane lines, one forward solid wedge, and one receding hashed dash.
Four forward solid wedges pointing equally toward the viewer.
Three in-plane lines forming a flat triangle and one receding hashed dash.
One in-plane line, two forward solid wedges, and one receding hashed dash.
questions.explanation: Any two bonds of a tetrahedron define a flat plane (two plain lines), leaving one bond projecting forward (wedge) and one receding backward (dash).

questions.prompt: When drawing a tetrahedral center cleanly, where should the solid wedge and hashed dash be placed relative to the two in-plane lines?
choices: Tucked snugly inside the narrowest pinch between the two in-plane lines.
Drawn directly on top of the two in-plane lines so they overlap.
Placed on opposite sides of the central atom at $$180^\circ$$ apart.
Placed side-by-side on the wide open outside of the in-plane V.
questions.explanation: In a real tetrahedron, the two out-of-plane bonds emerge from the wide outside of the $$109.5^\circ$$ in-plane V, keeping all four bonds evenly spaced.

chunks.title: The Rotation Illusion: Dichloromethane's Identical Twins
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a classic 3D puzzle that catches almost every beginner once—and then clicks forever. Look at dichloromethane ($$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$$), a tetrahedral carbon bonded to two hydrogens and two chlorines. Suppose one student draws both chlorines on plain in-plane lines (up and down-left), while a second student draws one chlorine on a forward solid wedge and the other chlorine on a plain line.

Are those two different molecules? If $$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$$ were a flat 2D square, putting two chlorines 'next to each other' versus 'across from each other' really would create two distinct shapes. But in a 3D tetrahedron, **every** corner sits at the exact same $$109.5^\circ$$ angle from **every** other corner! There is no 'across' position in a tetrahedron—every pair of bonds is adjacent. Simply rotating the first drawing slightly in your hand turns it seamlessly into the second drawing; they are two snapshots of the exact same molecule.

questions.prompt: Two drawings of tetrahedral $$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$$ place the chlorine atoms on different combinations of lines, wedges, and dashes. What is the relationship between them?
choices: They represent two chemically distinct molecules with different boiling points.
They are two different camera angles of the exact same 3D molecule.
Only the drawing with both chlorines on in-plane lines is physically possible.
The wedge-and-dash version is a flat square, while the plain-line version is tetrahedral.
questions.explanation: Because all four positions in a regular tetrahedron are mutually adjacent at $$109.5^\circ$$, any pair of chlorine placements can be rotated into any other.

questions.prompt: Why does putting two chlorines 'opposite' each other fail to create a second, different version of $$\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$$?
choices: Chlorine atoms refuse to bond to carbon unless they sit at $$90^\circ$$.
Hydrogen atoms constantly swap places with chlorine atoms every millisecond.
Wedge-and-dash drawings cannot display chlorine atoms on dashed bonds.
In a 3D tetrahedron, all four corners are equivalent and equally adjacent.
questions.explanation: Unlike a flat square (which has $$90^\circ$$ adjacent and $$180^\circ$$ opposite corners), every pair of corners in a tetrahedron shares the exact same $$109.5^\circ$$ separation.

chunks.title: Reading Molecules Like Sculptures
chunks.content_markdown:
With wedge-and-dash projections in your toolkit, flat pages can no longer fool you into seeing flat molecules. Whenever you glance at a chemical structure in an article or textbook, let the three strokes immediately lift the molecule off the page in your imagination: plain lines anchor the flat canvas, solid wedges leap toward your fingertips, and hashed dashes drift quietly into the background. Better still, remember that molecules tumble freely in space—so never freeze a wedge-and-dash sketch into one rigid pose.

So far, we have treated every angle inside a 4-domain tetrahedron as a neat, textbook $$109.5^\circ$$, whether the domains are bonds or lone pairs. Yet careful measurements reveal a curious twist: water's bond angle is not $$109.5^\circ$$—it is pinched down to $$104.5^\circ$$! In Section 5, we uncover the physical reason why lone pairs and multiple bonds squeeze neighboring angles.

questions.prompt: Which visual habit best helps you read any unfamiliar wedge-and-dash drawing accurately?
choices: Treat every solid wedge as a shorter bond and every hashed dash as a longer bond.
Assume that molecules stay permanently locked in the exact angle drawn on paper.
Use plain lines as the flat reference plane while picturing wedges forward and dashes back.
Ignore wedges and dashes altogether and flatten every angle back to $$90^\circ$$.
questions.explanation: Plain lines establish the plane of the page, while solid wedges project forward and hashed dashes recede behind it, reconstructing the rotatable 3D shape.

questions.prompt: You see a wedge-and-dash drawing of ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) with nitrogen at the top, one $$\text{N}-\text{H}$$ plain line angling down-left, one solid wedge down-right, and one hashed dash down-back. Where is nitrogen's lone pair pointing?
choices: Straight upward above the nitrogen atom, completing the tetrahedral electron-domain frame.
Flat along the bottom, sandwiched between the three hydrogen atoms.
Inside the nitrogen nucleus where it takes up zero three-dimensional space.
Directly through the forward solid wedge toward the front hydrogen atom.
questions.explanation: With the three bonds forming the downward tripod legs of the tetrahedron, nitrogen's invisible lone pair occupies the fourth tetrahedral position pointing upward.

sections.title: 5. Squeezing the Angles: Lone-Pair Compression & Multiple-Bond Spread
sections.summary: Explore why real molecular angles pinch slightly away from ideal geometric frameworks. Because a lone pair is tethered to only one nucleus, its cloud spreads wider and sits closer to the central atom than a bonding pair stretched between two nuclei—driving the classic angle squeeze from $$\text{CH}_4$$ ($$109.5^\circ$$) to $$\text{NH}_3$$ ($$107^\circ$$) to $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ ($$104.5^\circ$$), alongside the gentler broadening push of electron-rich multiple bonds.

chunks.title: The Case of the Shrinking Bond Angles
chunks.content_markdown:
Line up three familiar 4-domain molecules side by side and inspect their experimentally measured bond angles. Methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$) has four single bonds and zero lone pairs, and every $$\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{H}$$ angle hits an exact, textbook $$109.5^\circ$$. Swap one bond for a lone pair to get ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$), and the $$\text{H}-\text{N}-\text{H}$$ angles pinch slightly inward to $$107^\circ$$. Swap a second bond for another lone pair to get water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$), and the $$\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H}$$ angle squeezes even tighter down to $$104.5^\circ$$!

Every single one of these three molecules shares the exact same steric number of $$4$$ and the exact same tetrahedral electron-domain geometry. So why does the bond angle drop by roughly $$2.5^\circ$$ every time a lone pair replaces a bonded atom? The clue lies in comparing the actual shape of a bonding electron cloud against a lone-pair cloud.

questions.prompt: What pattern appears across the measured bond angles of $$\text{CH}_4$$ ($$109.5^\circ$$), $$\text{NH}_3$$ ($$107^\circ$$), and $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ ($$104.5^\circ$$)?
choices: Each added lone pair widens the remaining bond angles by about $$2.5^\circ$$.
Each added lone pair compresses the remaining bond angles by about $$2.5^\circ$$.
All three molecules keep identical $$109.5^\circ$$ angles regardless of lone pairs.
Only molecules with zero lone pairs experience any Coulomb repulsion.
questions.explanation: Replacing bonding pairs with lone pairs across the 4-domain series steadily pinches the remaining bond angles from $$109.5^\circ$$ to $$107^\circ$$ to $$104.5^\circ$$.

questions.prompt: Why is the shrinking angle progression from $$\text{CH}_4$$ to $$\text{NH}_3$$ to $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ initially surprising under basic balloon VSEPR?
choices: Because all three molecules have different steric numbers ranging from $$2$$ to $$4$$.
Because methane actually contains more lone pairs on carbon than water contains.
Because water is a linear molecule whose ideal bond angle should be $$180^\circ$$.
Because four identical balloon domains should keep every angle fixed at $$109.5^\circ$$.
questions.explanation: Simple identical-balloon VSEPR predicts $$109.5^\circ$$ for every 4-domain center, so the systematic inward pinch signals that lone-pair clouds are bulkier than bonding clouds.

chunks.title: Stretched Rubber Band vs. Puffed-Out Cloud
chunks.content_markdown:
To understand why lone pairs shove harder than bonds, compare the **bonding-pair vs. lone-pair spatial footprint**. Picture a bonding pair of electrons first. Those two negatively charged electrons sit between **two** positively charged atomic nuclei—one at the center and one on the outer neighbor. Pulled from both ends like a rubber band stretched tightly between two wooden pegs, a bonding electron cloud stays relatively long, taut, and slender.

Now snip away that outer nucleus so you are left with a lone pair. Tethered to only **one** central nucleus with no second positive anchor pulling it thin, that negative electron cloud relaxes outward, spreads much wider sideways, and hugs closer to the central atom's surface—more like an overinflated, stubby pear-shaped balloon crowding the knot. Because a lone pair occupies a wider angular footprint right next to the center, it exerts stronger Coulomb repulsion on every neighboring domain.

questions.prompt: Physically, why does a lone pair occupy a wider, closer spatial footprint around a central atom than a bonding pair?
choices: A lone pair contains three negatively charged electrons instead of two.
A lone pair is attracted by only one nucleus rather than stretched thin between two nuclei.
A lone pair carries a positive electric charge that expands away from the nucleus.
A bonding pair is pushed completely outside the atom's valence shell.
questions.explanation: Without a second outer nucleus pulling it taut into a slender bridge, a lone pair spreads wider laterally and hugs closer to the central atom.

questions.prompt: In our physical analogy, how does a bonding electron pair compare to a lone pair?
choices: A bonding pair resembles a wide pear, while a lone pair resembles a taut band.
Both clouds share the exact same width and length in every 3D direction.
A bonding pair resembles a slender band, while a lone pair resembles a wider pear.
A bonding pair sits inside the nucleus, while a lone pair floats between atoms.
questions.explanation: Two nuclei stretch a bonding cloud slender like a taut rubber band, whereas one nucleus lets a lone pair puff wider and hug closer to the center.

chunks.title: Walking Down the Classic Angle Ladder
chunks.content_markdown:
Now replay our three 4-domain molecules with this upgraded picture of **lone-pair angle compression**—the pinching of bond angles caused by bulky lone pairs elbowing slender bonding pairs slightly closer together. In methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$), all four domains are identical slender $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bonding clouds, so the push is perfectly balanced in every direction and every angle locks at $$109.5^\circ$$.

In ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$), one fat lone pair sits at the top of the tripod. Pushing downward harder than a slender bond ever could, it nudges the three $$\text{N}-\text{H}$$ legs slightly inward until they settle at $$107^\circ$$. In water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$), **two** plump lone pairs press against each other and against the two $$\text{O}-\text{H}$$ bonds simultaneously, pinching the $$\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H}$$ angle even tighter to $$104.5^\circ$$. The same rule works for 3-domain frames too: in bent $$\text{SO}_2$$, sulfur's single lone pair gently nudges the $$\text{O}-\text{S}-\text{O}$$ angle slightly below the ideal $$120^\circ$$ (to about $$119^\circ$$).

questions.prompt: Why is the $$\text{H}-\text{O}-\text{H}$$ angle in water ($$104.5^\circ$$) smaller than the $$\text{H}-\text{N}-\text{H}$$ angle in ammonia ($$107^\circ$$)?
choices: Water has two bulky lone pairs compressing its bonds, whereas ammonia has only one.
Oxygen atoms have fewer valence electrons than nitrogen atoms.
Water sits on a 3-domain framework while ammonia sits on a 4-domain framework.
Hydrogen atoms attract each other strongly in water but repel each other in ammonia.
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen create even greater lone-pair angle compression than the single lone pair on nitrogen, squeezing water's bonds further inward.

questions.prompt: Using lone-pair angle compression, what would you predict for the $$\text{O}-\text{S}-\text{O}$$ bond angle in bent sulfur dioxide ($$\text{SO}_2$$, steric number $$3$$, one lone pair)?
choices: Exactly $$180^\circ$$ because there are only two outer oxygen atoms.
Slightly greater than $$120^\circ$$ because the lone pair pulls the bonds outward.
Slightly less than $$120^\circ$$ because the lone pair pinches the two bonds slightly closer.
Exactly $$90^\circ$$ because sulfur atoms always lock into right angles.
questions.explanation: Starting from the $$120^\circ$$ trigonal planar framework, sulfur's single lone pair compresses the two bonding domains slightly below $$120^\circ$$.

chunks.title: A Gentler Push: Multiple-Bond Repulsion Broadening
chunks.content_markdown:
Lone pairs are not the only electron clouds with extra girth. Think back to formaldehyde ($$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$), our flat trigonal planar molecule with two single $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bonds and one $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bond. Even though that double bond counts as just one electron domain, it still packs **four** negatively charged electrons into the corridor between carbon and oxygen—twice as many negative charges as each single $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bond.

That thicker negative cloud creates **multiple-bond repulsion broadening**: a double or triple bond pushes neighboring single bonds slightly farther away than a single bond would. In formaldehyde, the plump $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ domain opens both $$\text{O}=\text{C}-\text{H}$$ angles slightly wider than $$120^\circ$$ (to roughly $$122^\circ$$) while squeezing the remaining $$\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{H}$$ angle slightly narrower (to roughly $$116^\circ$$). Because a multiple bond is still stretched between two nuclei, its extra shove is gentler than a lone pair's—giving a clean physical ranking: lone pair $$>$$ multiple bond $$>$$ single bond.

questions.prompt: In formaldehyde ($$\text{H}_2\text{CO}$$), why are the $$\text{O}=\text{C}-\text{H}$$ angles slightly wider than $$120^\circ$$ while the $$\text{H}-\text{C}-\text{H}$$ angle is slightly narrower?
choices: The carbon atom carries an unshared lone pair tucked between the hydrogens.
Oxygen nuclei physically collide with hydrogen nuclei whenever angles reach $$120^\circ$$.
Formaldehyde actually holds a steric number of $$4$$ rather than $$3$$.
The electron-rich $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bond pushes the single $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bonds closer.
questions.explanation: A double bond packs four shared electrons into its bonding corridor, so it pushes the two single $$\text{C}-\text{H}$$ bonds slightly closer together.

questions.prompt: Which ranking orders electron-domain repulsion strength from strongest to weakest?
choices: Single bond $$>$$ multiple bond $$>$$ lone pair.
Multiple bond $$>$$ lone pair $$>$$ single bond.
Lone pair $$>$$ multiple bond $$>$$ single bond.
Lone pair $$>$$ single bond $$>$$ multiple bond.
questions.explanation: An untethered lone pair spreads widest near the center, a multiple bond packs extra charge between two nuclei, and a single bond has the slimmest cloud.

chunks.title: Intuition Over Decimals
chunks.content_markdown:
Notice something liberating about everything we just learned: you do not need to memorize a giant table of exact decimal bond angles to think like a chemist! Just start from the clean ideal angle of the electron-domain framework—$$180^\circ$$, $$120^\circ$$, or $$109.5^\circ$$—and then ask a single physical question: are all the surrounding electron clouds equally plump?

If every domain is identical, the angles stay exact. If a wider lone pair sits on the central atom, the remaining bond angles pinch slightly below the ideal value. If an electron-rich double bond shares space with single bonds, angles next to the double bond open slightly wider while single-bond angles pinch slightly tighter. Every subtle tilt traces right back to Coulomb repulsion. Next, in Section 6, we will step briefly beyond four domains for a light, zero-memorization tour of the striking 5- and 6-domain shapes built by larger atoms like phosphorus and sulfur.

questions.prompt: In phosgene ($$\text{Cl}_2\text{CO}$$, a trigonal planar molecule with one $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bond and two $$\text{C}-\text{Cl}$$ single bonds), what do you predict for the $$\text{Cl}-\text{C}-\text{Cl}$$ angle?
choices: Slightly greater than $$120^\circ$$ because single bonds repel harder than double bonds.
Exactly $$109.5^\circ$$ because carbon atoms always enforce tetrahedral bond angles.
Exactly $$180^\circ$$ because the two chlorine atoms push straight opposite.
Slightly less than $$120^\circ$$ because the $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bond pinches the single bonds.
questions.explanation: Like formaldehyde, phosgene has steric number $$3$$; the electron-rich $$\text{C}=\text{O}$$ double bond broadens the $$\text{O}=\text{C}-\text{Cl}$$ angles and pinches the $$\text{Cl}-\text{C}-\text{Cl}$$ angle slightly below $$120^\circ$$.

questions.prompt: Why do chemists treat $$109.5^\circ$$ as an 'ideal' baseline rather than a rigid law for all 4-domain molecules?
choices: Because tetrahedral geometry occurs only in pure liquid water.
Because VSEPR repulsion breaks down whenever hydrogen atoms are absent.
Because exact symmetry holds only when all four surrounding domains repel equally.
Because bond angles drift randomly between $$90^\circ$$ and $$180^\circ$$ every second.
questions.explanation: When all four domains are equivalent (as in $$\text{CH}_4$$), angles sit at $$109.5^\circ$$; replacing bonds with wider lone pairs shifts the angles slightly from that ideal baseline.

sections.title: 6. Beyond Four Domains: A Light Tour of Five- and Six-Domain Shapes
sections.summary: Take a relaxed, zero-memorization conceptual tour of expanded-octet molecules with 5 and 6 electron domains. See how 5 domains in $$\text{PF}_5$$ divide into crowded $$90^\circ$$ axial poles and roomier $$120^\circ$$ equatorial belt sites—explaining why extra lone pairs always prefer the spacious equator—while 6 domains in $$\text{SF}_6$$ settle into a perfectly symmetric, all-$$90^\circ$$ octahedral framework.

chunks.title: When Atoms Break Past Four Domains
chunks.content_markdown:
Carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen—the headline stars of organic and biological molecules—almost never exceed four electron domains. Their compact outer shells fit comfortably around an **octet** (eight valence electrons, or four electron pairs), so steric numbers $$2$$, $$3$$, and $$4$$ cover virtually all of biochemistry. Yet stroll one row farther down the periodic table to larger atoms like phosphorus and sulfur, and you meet molecules that comfortably host five or six electron domains—a setup chemists call an **expanded octet**.

Two textbook celebrities are phosphorus pentafluoride ($$\text{PF}_5$$, five single bonds around phosphorus) and sulfur hexafluoride ($$\text{SF}_6$$, six single bonds around sulfur—a dense, harmless gas famously able to float tiny aluminum-foil boats on invisible air). You do not need to memorize a sprawling inorganic shape chart here; instead, let us apply our exact same balloon-repulsion intuition to see what happens when five or six clouds fight for room.

questions.prompt: Why can atoms like phosphorus ($$\text{PF}_5$$) and sulfur ($$\text{SF}_6$$) host five or six electron domains while carbon and oxygen almost never do?
choices: Phosphorus and sulfur lack electrostatic repulsion between their outer valence electrons.
Fluorine atoms carry no electrons and therefore occupy zero physical volume.
Carbon and oxygen are physically unable to form covalent bonds with fluorine.
Larger third-row atoms have roomier outer shells capable of expanded octets.
questions.explanation: Second-row elements like carbon and oxygen cap out at four electron pairs, whereas larger third-row elements like phosphorus and sulfur can accommodate five or six domains.

questions.prompt: What are the steric numbers of phosphorus in $$\text{PF}_5$$ and sulfur in $$\text{SF}_6$$, assuming zero lone pairs on each central atom?
choices: $$4$$ and $$4$$, because VSEPR caps every steric number at four.
$$5$$ and $$6$$, matching their five and six single-bond electron domains.
$$10$$ and $$12$$, counting every single valence electron as one domain.
$$3$$ and $$4$$, because only outer fluorine atoms count toward steric number.
questions.explanation: With zero lone pairs on the center, five single bonds give $$\text{PF}_5$$ steric number $$5$$ and six single bonds give $$\text{SF}_6$$ steric number $$6$$.

chunks.title: Five Domains and the Globe Split: Poles vs. Equator
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a wonderful geometric surprise: in three-dimensional space, you can arrange $$2$$, $$3$$, or $$4$$ points so every single point is completely identical—but it is geometrically impossible to arrange **five** points on a sphere identically! Tie five balloons together, and they spontaneously split into two distinct neighborhoods, just like a globe of Earth.

Three balloons fan out evenly around the middle waist at roomy $$120^\circ$$ angles, forming a flat central triangle; the remaining two balloons poke straight up through the North Pole and straight down through the South Pole at $$90^\circ$$ to the waist. Chemists call this 5-domain framework **trigonal bipyramidal geometry** (literally two three-sided pyramids glued base-to-base). The two pole sites and three waist sites define **axial vs. equatorial positions**: the axial positions run along the vertical axis from pole to pole, while the equatorial positions ring the middle equator.

questions.prompt: How are the five electron domains arranged in trigonal bipyramidal geometry?
choices: Five domains arranged in a flat five-pointed star with $$72^\circ$$ angles.
Four domains forming a flat square base with one domain pointing straight upward.
Three equatorial domains in a $$120^\circ$$ middle belt and two axial domains at the poles.
Two equatorial domains at $$180^\circ$$ and three axial domains crowded at one pole.
questions.explanation: A trigonal bipyramid splits five domains into three $$120^\circ$$ equatorial positions around the waist and two axial positions pointing along the vertical axis.

questions.prompt: What makes trigonal bipyramidal geometry fundamentally different from linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral frameworks?
choices: Its five domains attract one another instead of experiencing Coulomb repulsion.
Its bond angles are all identical at exactly $$109.5^\circ$$ around the center.
Its atoms must all lie completely flat inside a single two-dimensional sheet.
Its five positions are inequivalent, splitting into distinct axial and equatorial sites.
questions.explanation: Whereas every site in linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral shapes is identical, 5-domain geometry has two inequivalent site types: axial and equatorial.

chunks.title: Why Crowded Poles Send Lone Pairs to the Equator
chunks.content_markdown:
Look closely at phosphorus pentafluoride ($$\text{PF}_5$$) to compare how crowded an axial site feels versus an equatorial site. Stand on the North Pole (an axial fluorine) and look at your closest neighbors: all **three** equatorial bonds sit right beside you at a cramped $$90^\circ$$ angle! That means every axial domain endures three tight $$90^\circ$$ neighbors.

Now hop down to the waist (an equatorial fluorine) and count your tight $$90^\circ$$ neighbors. Only **two** bonds—the North Pole and the South Pole—sit at $$90^\circ$$ from you! Your other two equatorial neighbors lounge comfortably $$120^\circ$$ away around the belt. Because Coulomb repulsion drops off sharply as angles widen from $$90^\circ$$ to $$120^\circ$$, the equatorial belt is significantly roomier than the crowded axial poles. Instantly, with zero chart memorization, you can predict where any bulky lone pair will go in a 5-domain molecule: it **always** claims an equatorial seat first to escape those three cramped $$90^\circ$$ neighbors!

questions.prompt: In a trigonal bipyramidal molecule like $$\text{PF}_5$$, why is an equatorial position less crowded than an axial position?
choices: An equatorial domain has only two close $$90^\circ$$ neighbors, whereas an axial domain has three.
An equatorial domain sits farther away from the central nucleus by double the bond length.
An axial domain has four close $$90^\circ$$ neighbors, whereas an equatorial domain has none.
An equatorial domain sits at $$180^\circ$$ from every other domain in the molecule.
questions.explanation: An axial site faces three $$90^\circ$$ equatorial neighbors, whereas an equatorial site faces only two $$90^\circ$$ axial neighbors (with its other two neighbors at a roomy $$120^\circ$$).

questions.prompt: If a 5-domain central atom has four bonds and one bulky lone pair, where does that lone pair preferentially sit?
choices: At the North axial pole so it can push straight downward on all three belt bonds.
In one of the roomier equatorial belt positions to minimize tight $$90^\circ$$ repulsions.
Equally likely at an axial or equatorial position because both feel identical repulsion.
Halfway between an axial pole and an equatorial site at a $$45^\circ$$ slant.
questions.explanation: Because lone pairs spread wider than bonding pairs, placing them in an equatorial position avoids having three cramped $$90^\circ$$ neighbors.

chunks.title: Six Domains Restore Perfect Symmetry: The Octahedron
chunks.content_markdown:
Now tie a sixth balloon into the knot, as in sulfur hexafluoride ($$\text{SF}_6$$), and watch a geometric miracle unfold: all that 5-domain awkwardness vanishes, and flawless symmetry snaps right back! Six electron domains point straight along the six cardinal directions of 3D space—up, down, left, right, front, and back—like the six faces of a die or three perpendicular axes meeting at the center.

Chemists call this **octahedral geometry**. Why 'octa-' (eight) when there are only six bonds? Imagine stretching flat triangles across the six outer fluorine tips: four triangular faces on the top pyramid plus four triangular faces on the bottom pyramid create an eight-faced solid called an octahedron! Best of all, every single corner of an octahedron is 100% identical—each bond has four neighbors at exactly $$90^\circ$$ and one partner directly across at $$180^\circ$$. There is no difference between poles and equator anymore!

questions.prompt: Why is the 6-domain geometry of $$\text{SF}_6$$ called 'octahedral' even though only six outer atoms surround the sulfur?
choices: Because sulfur always carries two invisible lone pairs in addition to six bonds.
Because connecting the six outer atomic corners creates a 3D solid with eight triangular faces.
Because the ideal angle between every adjacent bond is $$80^\circ$$.
Because sulfur hexafluoride contains eight total valence electrons in its outer shell.
questions.explanation: The six vertices of the molecule outline an octahedron—two square pyramids joined base-to-base, giving eight flat triangular faces.

questions.prompt: How do the six bond positions in octahedral $$\text{SF}_6$$ compare to the five positions in trigonal bipyramidal $$\text{PF}_5$$?
choices: $$\text{SF}_6$$ has tighter equatorial angles than axial angles, whereas $$\text{PF}_5$$ is symmetric.
Both $$\text{SF}_6$$ and $$\text{PF}_5$$ have two distinct kinds of adjacent bond angles.
$$\text{SF}_6$$ sits completely flat in one plane, whereas $$\text{PF}_5$$ is three-dimensional.
All six sites in $$\text{SF}_6$$ are equivalent, whereas $$\text{PF}_5$$ has two site types.
questions.explanation: In an octahedron, rotating the molecule swaps any corner cleanly into any other corner (all adjacent angles are $$90^\circ$$), unlike the inequivalent sites of a trigonal bipyramid.

chunks.title: From Single Centers to Real-World Molecular Chains
chunks.content_markdown:
That wraps up our light conceptual tour of expanded-octet 3D space—no rote memorization of obscure inorganic nicknames required! Just hold onto the physical contrast: five domains in $$\text{PF}_5$$ cannot treat every site equally, so they split into crowded $$90^\circ$$ axial poles and roomier $$120^\circ$$ equatorial seats, whereas six domains in $$\text{SF}_6$$ restore total symmetry along the six compass directions of 3D space.

Notice one limitation we have kept throughout Sections 1 through 6: every molecule we analyzed had just **one** central atom! Real organic and biological molecules—from rubbing alcohol and vinegar to the proteins building your muscles—link dozens or thousands of atoms together into sprawling chains and rings. How do you find the 3D shape of a big molecule when there is no single 'center'? Section 7 reveals the simple secret: chain VSEPR one local atom at a time.

questions.prompt: If a 6-domain octahedral atom replaces one bond with a single lone pair, does it matter which of the six positions the lone pair takes first?
choices: Yes—it must pick one of the four flat equatorial sites instead of the poles.
Yes—it must pick the top axial pole to maximize separation from the equator.
No—all six octahedral sites are completely equivalent by symmetry.
No—because lone pairs cannot exist on atoms with six electron domains.
questions.explanation: Because every corner of an octahedron has the exact same four $$90^\circ$$ neighbors and one $$180^\circ$$ opposite neighbor, all six starting positions are identical.

questions.prompt: Which pair of steric numbers both produce completely equivalent, symmetric outer positions when all surrounding domains are identical?
choices: Steric numbers $$4$$ (tetrahedral) and $$6$$ (octahedral).
Steric numbers $$4$$ (tetrahedral) and $$5$$ (trigonal bipyramidal).
Steric numbers $$5$$ (trigonal bipyramidal) and $$6$$ (octahedral).
Steric numbers $$3$$ (trigonal planar) and $$5$$ (trigonal bipyramidal).
questions.explanation: Steric numbers $$2$$, $$3$$, $$4$$, and $$6$$ have completely equivalent positions, whereas steric number $$5$$ uniquely splits into inequivalent axial and equatorial sites.

sections.title: 7. Chaining Local Shapes: 3D Architecture of Multi-Center Molecules
sections.summary: Scale VSEPR from tiny single-center molecules to real organic and biological structures by diagnosing one interior atom at a time and chaining those local geometries together. Walk atom by atom through ethanol ($$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$), acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$), and the rigid, flat amide and peptide units—where resonance delocalization from Part III locks the nitrogen planar to sculpt protein backbones.

chunks.title: What If There Is No Single Central Atom?
chunks.content_markdown:
Every molecule we have shaped so far—$$\text{CO}_2$$, $$\text{CH}_4$$, $$\text{NH}_3$$, $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$, $$\text{PF}_5$$, and $$\text{SF}_6$$—was polite enough to have just one central atom sitting neatly in the middle. Now look at real molecules from your kitchen and your bloodstream: ethanol ($$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$, the alcohol in hand sanitizer), acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$, the tangy bite in vinegar), or a protein strand linking hundreds of atoms end to end.

None of those molecules has a single central atom! Instead, they are built from chains of several interior atoms bonded one after another. Does VSEPR break down the moment a molecule grows larger than a handful of atoms? Not at all—in fact, scaling VSEPR up to huge organic and biological architectures requires zero new rules, just one shift in perspective.

questions.prompt: Why do organic molecules like ethanol ($$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$) require a slightly different VSEPR approach than methane ($$\text{CH}_4$$)?
choices: They contain multiple interior atoms linked together rather than one single central atom.
They obey magnetic forces instead of Coulomb repulsion between electron clouds.
They flatten completely into two-dimensional sheets once they exceed five atoms.
They lack valence electrons on any atom other than oxygen.
questions.explanation: Larger organic molecules have several bonded interior atoms, so you apply VSEPR locally to each interior atom in turn rather than looking for one center.

questions.prompt: What happens to the core VSEPR repulsion rules when moving from small single-center molecules to large biological molecules?
choices: Every single bond suddenly counts as two separate electron domains.
Lone pairs lose their spatial footprint and stop repelling neighboring bonds.
The exact same local domain-counting rules continue to apply at every interior atom.
Steric numbers automatically jump to $$5$$ or $$6$$ on every carbon atom.
questions.explanation: Coulomb repulsion acts locally around every interior atom, so the exact same VSEPR principles scale smoothly to molecules of any size.

chunks.title: Snap-Together Hinges and the Zig-Zag Carbon Backbone
chunks.content_markdown:
The secret to shaping any large molecule is **local molecular geometry (multi-center chaining)**: zoom in on one interior atom at a time, count its own bonding domains and lone pairs, determine its local 3D shape, and then step to the next bonded atom and repeat. Think of a large molecule like a set of snap-together plastic hinges—each interior atom sets the exact bend angle right at its own joint.

This local chaining immediately explains one of the most iconic sights in chemistry: the **tetrahedral carbon backbone (zig-zag chain)**. Whenever carbon atoms link into a chain using only single bonds, each carbon has four single-bond domains—a local tetrahedral angle of $$109.5^\circ$$. Because every carbon-to-carbon joint bends at $$109.5^\circ$$ instead of stretching straight at $$180^\circ$$, a chain of single-bonded carbons naturally alternates up-down-up-down in a crisp zig-zag ribbon rather than a rigid straight pole!

questions.prompt: Why does a chain of single-bonded carbon atoms naturally form a zig-zag backbone rather than a straight line?
choices: Because single-bonded carbons alternate between steric numbers $$2$$ and $$6$$ along the chain.
Because chemists draw zig-zags purely as decoration even though real chains are straight.
Because each carbon in the chain holds two lone pairs that force $$90^\circ$$ corners.
Because each single-bonded carbon is locally tetrahedral with $$109.5^\circ$$ rather than $$180^\circ$$ joints.
questions.explanation: Each carbon with four single bonds forms a local tetrahedral joint near $$109.5^\circ$$, forcing the connected carbon-carbon chain into a zig-zag pattern.

questions.prompt: How does multi-center chaining determine the 3D shape of a multi-atom organic molecule?
choices: By averaging all bond angles in the entire molecule into one single number.
By counting only the electron domains on the leftmost atom in the formula.
By diagnosing the local VSEPR geometry around each interior atom and linking those joints together.
By replacing every interior carbon atom with an equivalent 6-domain octahedron.
questions.explanation: Applying VSEPR locally to each interior atom in sequence reveals the angle at every joint, assembling the full 3D molecular shape.

chunks.title: Atom-by-Atom Walkthrough: Ethanol and Acetic Acid
chunks.content_markdown:
Let us practice multi-center chaining on two everyday molecules. First, walk left to right across **ethanol** ($$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$). Its first carbon ($$\text{CH}_3$$) has four single bonds and no lone pairs: **tetrahedral** ($$109.5^\circ$$). Its middle carbon ($$\text{CH}_2$$) also has four single bonds and no lone pairs: **tetrahedral** ($$109.5^\circ$$). Finally, its oxygen atom has two single bonds (to carbon and hydrogen) plus two lone pairs—a 4-domain **bent** joint near $$104.5^\circ$$, shaped just like water with one hydrogen swapped for a carbon chain!

Now walk across **acetic acid** ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$). Its left $$\text{CH}_3$$ carbon has four single bonds: **tetrahedral** ($$109.5^\circ$$). Step to the middle carbon (bonded to one carbon, one single-bonded $$\text{OH}$$ oxygen, and one double-bonded $$=\text{O}$$ oxygen): three electron domains and zero lone pairs make that entire hub flat **trigonal planar** (near $$120^\circ$$)! Finally, the $$\text{OH}$$ oxygen carries two single bonds and two lone pairs: **bent** right next to that flat hub.

questions.prompt: Walking left to right across the three interior atoms of ethanol ($$\text{C}-\text{C}-\text{O}$$ in $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$), what is the sequence of local molecular geometries?
choices: Linear, linear, and linear.
Tetrahedral, tetrahedral, and bent.
Trigonal planar, tetrahedral, and trigonal pyramidal.
Tetrahedral, trigonal planar, and linear.
questions.explanation: Both carbons have four single bonds (tetrahedral), while the oxygen has two single bonds and two lone pairs (bent, just like water).

questions.prompt: In acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$), what is the local molecular geometry around the middle carbon atom double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to two other atoms?
choices: Tetrahedral, because carbon always forms four total covalent bonds.
Linear, because oxygen atoms repel each other to $$180^\circ$$.
Trigonal planar, because two single bonds and one double bond give a steric number of $$3$$.
